core: Definition: many firms, differentiated (not identical) products, free entry and exit
Product differentiation gives each firm a downward-sloping perceived demand curve and a small amount of market power, so P > MC
Profit maximization at MR = MC; because demand slopes down, price exceeds marginal revenue and marginal cost
Short-run economic profit or loss is possible
Free entry and exit drive long-run economic profit to about zero, when the perceived demand curve is tangent to the average cost curve
Long-run result: excess capacity and P > MC (neither productively nor allocatively efficient) but real product variety
Non-price competition: branding, advertising, quality, variety; advertising shifts perceived demand out or makes it less elastic
Real examples: restaurants, clothing stores, coffee shops, gas stations
supporting: Four dimensions of product differentiation: physical aspects, location, intangible aspects, buyer perception
Historical origin: theory of imperfect competition developed independently in 1933 by Edward Chamberlin and Joan Robinson
One-line contrasts with the other three market structures
outOfScope: Deep treatment of perfect competition, monopoly, or oligopoly (their own topics)
Game theory and strategic interdependence (belongs to oligopoly)
Antitrust and price-fixing law (belongs to oligopoly)

claims.claim: Monopolistic competition is a market with many firms that sell products differentiated in some way, with free entry and exit.

Because its product is differentiated, a monopolistically competitive firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve: it can raise price without losing all customers or lower price to gain more, giving it a small amount of market power.
The firm maximizes profit where marginal revenue equals marginal cost; because demand slopes downward, price is higher than marginal revenue, so price exceeds marginal cost.
A monopolistically competitive firm can earn positive economic profit or take a loss in the short run.

Free entry (when firms earn profit) and exit (when they take losses) shift each firm's perceived demand curve until it is tangent to the average cost curve, at which point economic profit is zero in the long run.

At the long-run tangency the firm produces on the downward-sloping part of the average cost curve, not at its minimum, so it carries excess capacity; with price above marginal cost the outcome is neither productively nor allocatively efficient, though it delivers product variety.
Advertising and branding are forms of non-price competition; advertising can shift a firm's perceived demand curve outward or make it less elastic, raising the price or quantity the firm can achieve.
Firms differentiate products along four dimensions: physical aspects, selling location, intangible aspects, and buyer perception.
The theory of imperfect competition was developed independently in 1933 by Edward Chamberlin (The Economics of Monopolistic Competition) and Joan Robinson (The Economics of Imperfect Competition).
